c.text: Chapter 3 – Knowing Your Role
Most new-leader trouble is role trouble
Many first-year leadership conflicts grow out of unclear responsibilities. A role that has never been defined leaves room for misunderstandings about decisions, expectations and accountability.

You made a decision you thought was yours and discovered it wasn’t. You waited for permission on something everyone assumed you would just handle. You told a volunteer something the pastor had already told them differently. You were criticised for a decision you had no part in making.
Those examples may reflect unclear boundaries rather than poor character. This chapter helps you clarify who is responsible for what.
The centurion understood something the disciples didn’t
In Matthew 8:5-10 a Roman centurion comes to Jesus in Capernaum about a paralysed servant. Jesus offers to come to the house. The centurion says that isn’t necessary – just say the word.

Then he explains his reasoning in verse 9, and this is the part to sit with. He says that he himself is a man under authority, with soldiers under him; he tells one to go and he goes, another to come and he comes.
Notice the logic.

He does not say “I am a man with authority.” He says he is a man under it. His ability to command rests entirely on the fact that he stands inside a chain that goes up to Rome. When he gives an order, what makes it work is not his personality – it is the empire standing behind him.
Jesus calls this the greatest faith he has found in Israel. The centurion grasped, better than the religious professionals did, how spiritual authority actually works.
Apply that to yourself.

Whatever authority you carry in your ministry is delegated. It came down to you, it is not generated by you, and it operates only within the area it was given for. That is not a demotion. It is the only kind of authority that holds weight.
What Scripture asks of you toward your leaders

Hebrews 13:17 tells believers to obey their leaders and submit to them, because those leaders keep watch over their souls as people who must give an account – and it adds a reason that is easy to skip: so that they may do this with joy and not with grief, since that would be of no advantage to you.
The writer’s argument is practical, not authoritarian. Your pastor carries a weight of responsibility for people’s souls. Making that weight heavier costs everyone, including you.

1 Peter 5:1-5 speaks to both sides at once, and this balance matters. Peter, writing to scattered and suffering churches, tells elders to shepherd the flock willingly rather than under compulsion, eagerly rather than for dishonest gain, and – the key phrase – not lording it over those entrusted to them, but being examples. Then in verse 5 he tells the younger ones to submit to the elders, and tells all of them to clothe themselves with humility toward one another.

Read those together and you see leaders called to serve without domination, and a community called to humility and responsible cooperation. Respect does not require silence about wrongdoing. Accountability belongs on both sides.
And what Scripture does not ask of you
Submission is not silence, and it is not agreement.

Galatians 2:11-14 records Paul confronting Peter in Antioch – to his face, in public – because Peter had been eating with Gentile believers and then withdrew when a group came from James, and other Jewish believers followed his example. Paul calls it hypocrisy and says he opposed him because he stood condemned.
Peter was an apostle, senior to Paul in every visible way.
Paul still confronted him, because the issue was the truth of the gospel and Peter’s behaviour was pulling the church apart.

Acts 15 shows the same church handling a serious doctrinal dispute by gathering, arguing it out, listening to Peter, to Paul and Barnabas, and finally to James, and reaching a decision together. Vigorous disagreement, in the open, in the right room.

And Acts 15:36-40 is oddly comforting: Paul and Barnabas have a disagreement sharp enough that they part company over whether to take John Mark. Two godly men, unresolved conflict, and God used both of them afterwards.

The biblical picture allows serious questions and honest disagreement. Raise ordinary concerns constructively and avoid undermining decisions through gossip. Concerns about harm, coercion or misconduct may require a different reporting route and should never be suppressed for the sake of appearances.
The rebellion warning, used honestly

Numbers 16 tells of Korah, Dathan and Abiram challenging Moses and Aaron, joined by 250 community leaders. The account describes a grave rebellion and judgement; it needs to be read in its own setting.
That passage has been badly misused. It gets quoted at anyone who asks a hard question. So handle it carefully.

Numbers 16 describes a challenge to Moses and Aaron’s appointed roles, including Korah’s desire for the priesthood. It is not a simple template for every disagreement in a modern church. The account includes both the earth swallowing people and fire consuming the 250 offering incense.
Do not use a grievance to recruit allies against someone.

But asking for confidential advice, using a complaints process or reporting harm is not rebellion. It may be wise or necessary to seek help before approaching the person concerned, especially where there is a power imbalance or fear of retaliation.
Getting the boundary drawn in practice
Here is the conversation I would have you schedule with whoever you report to. Twenty minutes, four questions:

1. What decisions can I make alone? Get real examples – spending up to what amount, changing a meeting time, choosing songs, adding a volunteer. 2. What requires approval, and what requires prompt reporting? Clarify spending, teaching, appointments and changes of role. Safeguarding concerns must follow the reporting process; do not wait for a manager’s permission to raise them. 3. What do you want to hear about even when I’ve handled it? Complaints, a volunteer quitting, a pastoral situation in your team. 4. How do you want me to raise a disagreement, and when? Write the answers down and send them back afterwards: “Here is what I understand we agreed.” A clear record can prevent later misunderstandings.
When you disagree

For an ordinary, lawful decision within the team’s remit, a useful starting point is: discuss concerns honestly before the decision and implement the agreed outcome responsibly afterwards. This does not apply to concealing wrongdoing or preventing further review.
Explain your concern clearly, with reasons.
For an ordinary decision you can support in good conscience, implement the agreed outcome without undermining colleagues. Keep a suitable route open for review if new information emerges.
If you cannot in good conscience support it, say so directly to your pastor rather than to your team, and be willing to step back from that piece of the work.
One honest caution
Everything above assumes a leadership that is basically healthy – one that would welcome the four questions and hear a disagreement.
Some are not.

If questions bring punishment or you are asked to conceal harm, seek independent advice and use the appropriate reporting route. Do not wait for the implicated leader’s permission. Submission never requires covering wrongdoing.
If this describes your situation, take it seriously.
Do not let a misused passage keep you silent.
